description: Anadolu University student in Eskişehir, stubbornly curious. Systems software and data analysis; 12 merged contributions to NASA and CERN open-source projects, and a preprint with a DOI on NASA/IBM's Surya model. Plan: a Moon challenge on real mission data, not a mockup. Need: web interface, design, data visualization, English writing. Beginners welcome. TR/EN, Eskişehir. I finish what I start.
summary: Missions to the Moon's south pole rarely land exactly where and when they planned: dates slip, and landers come down tens to hundreds of metres from their targets. Near the pole either miss can trade weeks of sunlight for days of darkness. Tools that show the Sun and the Earth at one place and time exist, but asking what happens when the plan shifts means running them again and again. Forgiving Ground does those runs. Pick a site, a date and how long the lander lasts without sunlight, and it answers yes or no, with the margin: how many days the landing can slip and how far off target it can come down. It shows the Sun and the Earth over the real horizon from NASA LOLA terrain, with the time left to sunset and Earthrise, and a forgiveness map of 128,000 spots around the pole and on Mons Mouton. The engine behind every answer is checked against independent sources, most of them NASA's: the JPL Horizons System, NASA Goddard's polar illumination maps and a published study of the best lit ridges, which we match within 0.2 percentage points at three of its four points.
details:
What it does

The tool answers one question: if the landing slips, will the lander survive?

  • Pick a place and a date. A list of sites with sourced coordinates (the six Apollo landings, commercial landers, landers of ISRO and JAXA, an upcoming CLPS target, the best lit ridges near the south pole), any point clicked on a map within ten degrees of the pole, or typed coordinates. Then a landing date and a mission length from 6 days to a year.
  • See the sky. The whole horizon unrolled, with the Sun and the Earth now and their paths over the next lunar day, the next sunset or Earthset marked with its date, and the ridge that hides them.
  • Read the mission. A timeline of sunlight, Earth in view and neither; the longest darkness; the longest time without the Earth; the share of sunlight while the Earth is hidden, the question NASA's VIPER planners asked.
  • Read the answer. Yes or no: does the lander survive this landing? Then the margins: how many days the landing can move earlier or later, how far from the target it can end up (16 spots tested at each of four distances), and which of the date, the landing spot or the terrain map moves the answer most. Survival limits come from NASA documents: 50 hours (VIPER mission planning) and 85 and 150 hours (Lunar Surface Data Book).
  • Plan the date. The longest darkness for 120 landing days around the chosen one, and the landing windows that work over the next twelve months.
  • See the whole area. The forgiveness map colours a 250 m grid around the pole and on Mons Mouton by the share of a year's landing days on which a lander survives, for a chosen mission length, survival limit and landing accuracy.
  • Compare, keep and share. Add any place and date to a table that sets them side by side with the answer for each, save a scenario as CSV files, share it as a link.

How it works

  • Sun and Earth positions come from JPL's DE440 ephemeris and lunar orientation, read with NAIF SPICE and stored as small tables; the browser interpolates them, so the page needs no server.
  • The horizon of a place comes from NASA LOLA elevation models: 20 m near the pole, 80 m and 240 m further out, 720 directions. Outside the south polar cap the listed sites use SLDEM2015, which combines LOLA with images from JAXA's Kaguya. For points clicked near the pole the browser computes the horizon on the spot.
  • There is no atmosphere, so the horizon is the terrain or the edge of the Moon. The Sun counts as up while any part of its disc shows, and eclipses of the Sun by the Earth are included.
  • The forgiveness map was computed in advance for 128,000 points and 365 landing days each.

How we checked it

The validation table on the page shows each check next to its source.

  • 6,430 directions of the Sun and the Earth against the JPL Horizons System: largest difference 0.0002 degrees.
  • Sun angle at the Apollo landings against NASA's Apollo by the Numbers: within 0.35 degrees at five landings. At Apollo 16 the table gives the planned angle; the landing was six hours late, and we show why that moved the Sun by 3 degrees.
  • The eclipse of 14 March 2025 at the Blue Ghost Mission 1 site against the times Firefly Aerospace published: within one minute.
  • Daylight from touchdown to sunset for Blue Ghost Mission 1, with terrain: 347.1 hours against Firefly's 346.
  • The best lit ridges near the south pole against Gläser et al. (NASA NTRS 20170007365), at the same points, over the same twenty years: within 0.2 percentage points of sunlight and one hour of the longest shadow at three of four published points, two metres above the ground.
  • 150 random points against NASA Goddard's polar illumination maps: median difference 0.2 percentage points.
  • The forgiveness map against the page's own engine at random cells: 97% within 5 points.
  • The page against itself: in 40 test cases its table, cards and sentences agree with the engine in 336 of 336 checks, and in 32 cases its pictures agree with it pixel by pixel in 130 of 130.

Why it matters

NASA's site selection for its south polar landings favours regions with robust illumination across mission windows and reduced sensitivity to timing uncertainties (George et al., NASA NTRS 20250011660). The tool turns that criterion into numbers and a map anyone can read. It gives teams without NASA's internal tools, such as new lunar programmes, small companies and students, a quick and checked first look, and it shows teachers and the public why the south pole is hard, in six facts measured with the tool itself.

One finding: in the 80 km by 80 km square around the pole, only 0.38 km² of 6,400 km² lets a 14 day mission that survives 150 hours of darkness live through nine in ten landing days of a year; if the landing can be 250 m off, no spot does. And the two places that fail differ: on Shackleton's rim the date barely matters but 100 m does, while on Mons Mouton a kilometre barely matters but landing two days early does.

Limits

  • Terrain smaller than the map pixels (20 m near the pole) is not included. At ground level on a ridge the first tens of metres decide the answer, so the page works two metres above the ground by default.
  • Not included: lander tilt, panel pointing, temperature, relay satellites and ground station schedules.
  • Points clicked outside the south polar cap use a smooth Moon.

Tools

JavaScript (ES modules, Canvas), HTML and CSS for the page, with no third party library; the fonts Inter and Space Grotesk (SIL Open Font License) from Google Fonts. Python with NumPy, SpiceyPy, Rasterio (GDAL), Numba and Pillow to prepare the data. 31 automated tests in Node.js. AI: Claude (Anthropic), co-engineered with Kadir. What it did is stated in the next section and, in full, in AI_USE.md, published with the page (https://kadircanyildirm-crypto.github.io/kizil-boru/AI_USE.md).

Who did what

All code and data in the project were made during the hackathon. AI was utilized strictly as a coding assistant to accelerate implementation, while the core system architecture, algorithms, and final code integration were engineered and validated by Kadir.

Kadir Can Yıldırım put forward the core question that drives the whole project and designed the entire solution around it: what happens to the lander if the landing itself slips by a few days, or by a few hundred metres from the target? He led the project and directed the software work: what the tool must answer, what each part must show, and what stayed after each round of changes. Mina Yırtıcı was the team's decision-maker for design; she reviewed the interface as a first-time user and her judgement settled its final look. Kadir and the AI co-ideated the features, with the team deciding what to build, set what the project must not claim, and checked the AI's work: every number against an independent source, the tool by hand, and the page's pictures and words against its own numbers.
